question: Which animal was originally used to discover the Rhesus blood group system?
explanation: Researchers Landsteiner and Wiener used red blood cells from Rhesus monkeys during their foundational immunology experiments. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h1)

question: Why does an Rh-negative person usually not have anti-Rh antibodies in their blood at birth?

options.A: The body destroys these specific antibodies during fetal life
options.B: Rh antigens are identical in both positive and negative humans
options.C: Antibodies only form after exposure to Rh-positive cells
options.D: Placental barriers completely block the production of all globulins

explanation: Unlike the ABO system, Rh antibodies are immune antibodies that require a previous exposure to develop. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h1)

question: On which human chromosome are the main genes that control the Rh system located?
explanation: The RHD and RHCE genes sit close together on the short arm of chromosome 1. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h2)

question: What genetic change causes a person to have an Rh-negative blood type?

options.A: Suppression of the ABO transferase enzyme
options.C: Duplication of the RHCE gene complex
options.D: Deletion or mutation of the RHD gene

explanation: When the RHD gene is missing or altered so it cannot produce the D protein, the red blood cells lack the D antigen. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h2)

question: What does the 'd' factor in the Rh system actually represent?

options.A: It is an independent antigen located on chromosome 6
options.B: It is simply the absence of the D antigen
options.C: It is a weak recessive protein found in Africans
options.D: It represents a rare destructive antibody subtype

explanation: There is no actual 'd' protein. The symbol is used purely to show that the D antigen is missing. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h3)

question: Which of the following is NOT one of the main alleles tracked in the Rh system?
explanation: The primary alleles evaluated in standard Rh testing are C, c, D, E, and e. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h3)

question: Why is the D antigen considered the most critical factor in routine clinical blood banking?

options.A: It is the only blood antigen found in human newborns
options.B: It triggers a very strong immune response if mismatched
options.C: It changes its chemical structure based on body temperature
options.D: It neutralizes the natural antibodies of the ABO system

explanation: Out of all non-ABO antigens, D has the highest immunogenicity, meaning exposure easily prompts antibody creation. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h4)

question: What happens in a laboratory test when a patient's blood sample is genuinely Rh-positive?

options.A: The sample changes to a bright neon green color
options.B: A clear separation of clear plasma and white cells appears
options.C: The red blood cells completely dissolve in the solution
options.D: Agglutination occurs when mixed with anti-D serum

explanation: When anti-D antibodies meet D antigens on red cells, they bind together and cause visible clumping, or agglutination. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h4)

question: Which specific class of maternal antibody is small enough to cross the placenta and attack fetal red blood cells?
explanation: Immunoglobulin G (IgG) is the only antibody type capable of crossing the human placenta to enter fetal circulation. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h5)

question: When is an Rh-negative woman most likely to be exposed to fetal D antigens during her first pregnancy?

options.A: At the time of placental separation and delivery
options.B: Right after the first maternal heartbeat is detected
options.C: During the seventh week of embryonic organ formation
options.D: When morning sickness peaks in the first trimester

explanation: Most fetomaternal bleeding happens during the third stage of labor when the placenta separates from the uterine wall. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h5)

question: What is the primary medication used to prevent Rh sensitization in pregnant women?
explanation: Rh immunoglobulin neutralizes fetal red blood cells before the mother's immune system recognizes them, preventing sensitization. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h6)

question: Why is brain damage (kernicterus) a major risk for a newborn with severe hemolytic disease?

options.A: Massive red blood cell breakdown releases toxic levels of free bilirubin
options.B: Severe anemia cuts off oxygen supply to the respiratory center
options.C: The liver produces excessive amounts of toxic clotting proteins
options.D: Maternal antibodies directly destroy the infant brain neurons

explanation: Rapid red blood cell breakdown produces large amounts of unconjugated bilirubin, which can cross the newborn blood-brain barrier and cause permanent neurological damage. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h6)

question: Why is matching Rh status especially critical when giving blood transfusions to young female patients?

options.A: To stop the recipient's kidneys from filtering out platelets
options.B: To prevent sensitization that could threaten future pregnancies
options.C: To avoid immediate fatal clotting inside the heart chambers
options.D: To ensure normal bone marrow production of white blood cells

explanation: Exposing an Rh-negative girl or woman of childbearing age to Rh-positive blood can cause sensitization leading to hemolytic disease in later pregnancies. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h7)

question: Which blood product combination is an avoidable transfusion risk for an Rh-negative female of childbearing age?
explanation: Giving Rh-positive red cells to an Rh-negative woman of childbearing age risks creating permanent sensitization against the D antigen. [learn more](BMP111_U5_T7#BMP111_U5_T7_h7)
